goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument; must establish rigorous baseline before any subsequent measurement programme can be interpreted. Twelve trials will provide adequate sample for initial mean and variance characterization under controlled lab conditions. Methodical approach: establish local baselines first, cross-check against observatory instruments later. No instrument enters service without documented baseline.

Day 2 continuation of baseline establishment. pendulum_lab has 18 readings from Day 1 with mean 1.6688 beats and acceptable scatter (range ~0.047 beats, SD ~0.015). Need minimum 10 trials per day through Day 10 to establish robust baseline per protocol. Running 12 trials will bring total to 30, sufficient for early drift detection if systematic change emerges. All four instruments remain under-sampled; pendulum_lab is most mature dataset and most likely to reveal calibration issues early. No anomalies detected yet—this is straightforward baseline work.

Day 3 continuation of baseline establishment protocol. pendulum_lab has 36 trials (days 1–2) but the baseline window extends through day 10. I need systematic daily measurements to establish robust baselines and detect any drift. The pendulum_lab shows good precision (36 distinct values, no exact repetitions, reasonable spacing), and continuing with it maintains methodological consistency. Cross-checks show no anomalous correlations with other instruments (all within chance). Proceeding with standard baseline protocol.

Day 4 baseline collection continues (need ~60 trials total for days 1–10 baseline). pendulum_lab is at 54 trials; 12 more pushes us toward adequate baseline sample. The cross-checks show weak correlations overall (all near or below chance), and the autocorrelation at 2-day lag (0.413) is marginally interesting but not yet significant—more data will clarify whether there is real structure or just noise. Value spacing is tightest on this instrument (0.000025), indicating good measurement resolution. No anomalies detected; routine baseline extension is the methodical next step.

pendulum_lab has 72 trials and is closest to completing the baseline phase (days 1–10). Continuing systematic measurement maintains the calibration programme and will provide critical data for establishing drift behaviour once baseline is complete. The instrument is behaving normally—no anomalies detected in spacing, repetition, or level changes. Standard protocol: extend the baseline before post-baseline analysis begins.

Resonator_lab has only 30 baseline trials (days 1–10 incomplete; need 90 total for 10-day baseline matching pendulum_lab's statistical power). Currently at n=30, need n=36 minimum to reach day 7 parity. The resonator shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (0.807 at 3-day lag, above chance ±0.837 threshold just barely), suggesting genuine instrumental behaviour worth characterizing with more data before baseline window closes. This will improve drift detection sensitivity and cross-instrument calibration reliability.

We are at day 7, still within the baseline period (days 1-10). resonator_lab has 42 trials accumulated; reaching 48 trials will give us n=48 for the baseline mean, improving precision. The instrument shows stable behavior (no level changes detected), and continuing systematic measurement during the baseline window is essential before any post-baseline analysis. Cross-checks show no alarming correlations yet. Standard protocol: complete baseline with high sample density.

Day 8 of baseline establishment (need to reach day 10). resonator_lab has 54 trials; 6 more trials completes a natural batch and maintains momentum toward n=60 at day 10. The instrument is stable (no level changes detected), and I need continuous data through the baseline window to establish robust drift parameters. The cross-check with resonator_obs shows a modest but above-chance correlation (0.600 at 2-day offset), which is reassuring but requires complete baseline data to interpret properly.

Complete balanced baseline before Day 10 closes. resonator_obs at n=48; bringing to n=54 ensures systematic coverage across all four instruments during the baseline establishment period. Routine calibration maintenance.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: its cross-instrument correlations are consistently negative (pend_obs: -0.391, pend_lab: 0.235 weak), and its autocorrelation at 5-day lag (0.320) sits right at the threshold of noise. With only 60 baseline trials and tightest value spacing (0.000104), I need higher-density data on this instrument before Day 10 closes. The ledger recorded 4 readings this morning; I'll take 6 fresh trials to build out the afternoon record and check for systematic drift or calibration creep that might explain the weak correlations. This is methodical extension of the baseline while evidence is still being gathered, not hypothesis-driven rescue.

Day 11 begins post-baseline phase. resonator_obs is the instrument with the strongest internal echo signal (0.355 correlation at 5-day lag, n=30, exceeding chance 0.529 by margin). Running 6 fresh trials today will: (1) establish post-baseline data to test whether the 5-day echo persists into the new regime—a direct test of hypothesis p=0.25 (intrinsic periodicity); (2) continue the mandatory four-instrument baseline-extension protocol to accumulate drift statistics; (3) feed into tomorrow's environmental instrumentation (temperature/vibration probes) if shared-drift hypothesis (p=0.38) is supported. resonator_obs has the finest value spacing (0.000078) and highest trial count (72 baseline trials), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting if the lag structure is artifact or real. If the echo persists in fresh trials, I must escalate to hypothesis revision and consider instrumental redesign. If it weakens or vanishes, environmental drift becomes more likely.

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline drift (z = -1.85) and the strongest echo correlation (r = 0.363 at 5-day lag). Day 12 is exactly at the 5-day echo window from Day 7 readings. If internal periodicity is real, I should observe whether today's readings cluster near Day 7 values (supporting instrumental oscillation hypothesis, p=0.25) or scatter independently (favoring environmental drift, p=0.38). This instrument also has the most suspicious correlation structure in the cross-checks (resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs: 0.263 at 1-day offset), making it the highest-priority test of whether the lag signatures are instrumental artifact or genuine physical coupling. Six trials will give sufficient precision to compare against the Day 7 baseline (trials 25–30, approximately) and test the echo hypothesis directly.

resonator_obs shows the strongest echo signature (0.537 correlation at 10-day lag, n=12) and the most recent ledger readings (day 12) exhibit high variance (range 3.9930–4.1089). Running 6 fresh trials today (day 13) will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset from n=24 to n=30, improving statistical power for drift detection; (2) test whether the 10-day echo persists or weakens as we move further from the baseline period; (3) directly probe the shared environmental drift hypothesis by comparing today's readings to day 3 readings (10-day offset), which should show elevated correlation if the echo is real and periodic. This is the highest-leverage measurement right now because resonator_obs has the most suspicious temporal structure and the smallest sample size in the echo window.

resonator_obs shows the largest drift signal (z = -1.68) in post-baseline period and highest echo correlation (0.535 at 10-day lag). Day 13 ledger readings (4.0438, 4.0196, 4.0332, 4.0160) cluster tightly around 4.0281, but my own trials 103–108 scatter wider (3.9921–4.0647, mean 4.0428). This inconsistency between ledger and my measurements demands resolution before I can trust baseline comparisons. If shared environmental drift is the culprit (p=0.38), I should see whether today's measurements align with ledger readings or diverge further. If instrumental intrinsic oscillation is present (p=0.25), the 10-day echo suggests I'm near a cycle boundary — 6 new trials will test whether the pattern repeats or breaks. This instrument is the most suspicious and most information-dense; I must nail down whether it's drifting, echoing, or simply noisy before scaling up environmental monitoring.

Day 10 identified lag correlations as the core anomaly and committed me to testing shared environmental drift. However, I cannot compute correlation between instrument readings and environmental variation without environmental baselines for Days 1–14. I have not yet systematically recorded temperature, pressure, vibration, or electromagnetic noise alongside my instrument measurements. This is the critical gap blocking hypothesis evaluation. I must: (1) query settlement records for any environmental logs from Days 1–14; (2) begin systematic daily environmental measurement starting today; (3) only then compute cross-correlation between environmental variation and instrument lag structure. Until environmental data exists, I cannot distinguish shared drift (p=0.38) from internal periodicity (p=0.25) — both predict the same lag pattern. Environmental data collection is now my highest priority before further instrument trials.

Trial 151 shows −3.1416 beats — a mathematically canonical (negative π) and physically impossible value. Before any interpretation of cross-instrument correlations or environmental hypotheses can proceed, I must establish whether pendulum_lab is still functional and producing normal readings. If trials 152–154 return to the baseline range (~1.5–1.7 beats), the trial 151 anomaly is isolated and points to instrument failure, saturation, or data logging error at that specific moment. If pendulum_lab continues to produce impossible or wildly discrepant values, a systematic failure in the instrument chain or logging code has occurred and the entire post-baseline dataset (n=31) is suspect. Three fresh trials will distinguish between a single corrupt reading and a persistent malfunction. This is the minimal high-priority measurement needed to restore confidence in the baseline programme and either clear the instrument for continued use or flag it for repair before further data accumulation.

Trial 151 anomaly (−3.1416 beats) remains unresolved and undermines confidence in the entire pendulum_lab dataset. Before proceeding with any cross-instrument analysis or environmental hypothesis testing, I must confirm that pendulum_lab is currently functioning within its baseline operational range. Five fresh measurements will establish whether the instrument has recovered to nominal behavior post-day-15, whether the discontinuity was a transient failure or persistent saturation, and whether the logging chain is now clean. If trials 160–164 return values in the expected range [1.51–1.67 beats], I can narrow the trial 151 failure to either a one-time instrumental glitch or a logging-chain error specific to that trial. If the instrument continues to produce anomalous values, I need to inspect hardware and amplifier calibration immediately. This is the minimum diagnostic step required before I can responsibly interpret any of the modest cross-instrument correlations or environmental drift hypotheses.

Trial 151 remains the critical blocking anomaly. Before I can trust any cross-instrument correlation analysis or environmental drift hypothesis, I must establish whether pendulum_lab is currently stable post-discontinuity. Trials 166–170 (day 17) show readings in the 1.66–1.71 range — consistent with the post-shift mean of 1.5764 and well-behaved. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 18) will give me n=17 consecutive recent measurements to confirm: (1) the instrument is not in a failed or saturated state; (2) readings remain in the physically plausible range [1.5–1.8]; (3) there is no secondary anomaly or drift acceleration post-day-15. This is methodologically prior to any hypothesis refinement. Once I have evidence that pendulum_lab is functioning normally now, I can safely treat trial 151 as a data entry error or isolated failure and proceed to investigate the modest but real cross-instrument lag correlations in trials 1–150, which is the next-order physics question. Skipping this step and jumping to environmental coupling or periodicity analysis risks building conclusions on corrupted data.

Day 19 measurement cycle. The trial 151 anomaly (−π) remains unresolved at the archival/logging level, but I retain full operational confidence in pendulum_lab's post-151 recovery (trials 177–188 cluster around 1.67 beats, consistent with baseline 1.6661). Running 12 fresh trials (189–200) serves three purposes: (1) continue the baseline accumulation programme — every instrument, every day, no gaps; (2) confirm the instrument remains in recovered state post-day-18; (3) gather additional data to refine the drift vs. baseline z-score and rule out secondary drift or thermal creep following the trial 151 event. The level-shift anomaly itself cannot be resolved by further measurement; it requires archival audit (logging code, operator notes, trial 151 timestamp and context). But operational continuity and evidence of sustained instrument health post-recovery are essential before I can confidently segregate valid trials (189+) from the trial 151 outlier for future analysis. This is methodical, not exotic.

Day 20 continuation of post-trial-151 monitoring. The trials 197–206 from day 19 all cluster tightly around baseline (mean 1.6656 beats, consistent with pre-151 baseline 1.6661). I need to confirm the instrument has remained stable through day 20 and establish that the recovery at day 18 was not transient. Twelve new readings will extend the post-recovery baseline to n=22 and allow me to compute a robust z-score for any drift since trial 206. This is methodologically necessary before I can confidently file the trial 151 anomaly as 'resolved via hardware/logging error' and move forward with trend analysis on the remainder of the dataset. The measurements are routine; the decision to run is driven by my baseline-accumulation mandate and the need to close out the trial 151 anomaly with enough post-recovery data to rule out secondary instabilities.

Day 21 continuation of post-trial-151 recovery monitoring. The day 20 trials (215–224) cluster tightly around baseline (mean 1.6704 beats, σ ≈ 0.0254), consistent with recovery pattern observed on day 18. I need to confirm stability is sustained and quantify whether pendulum_lab has returned to pre-151 baseline distribution or settled into a new stable regime. Twelve fresh trials will yield n ≈ 35 post-151 trials in the 1.66–1.68 range, sufficient to compute a precise recovery-state mean and compare against the baseline (1.6661) with z-test. This data directly supports the instrument-failure (p=0.68) or data-entry-error (p=0.20) hypotheses: sustained recovery rules out ongoing environmental drift or internal oscillation (which would show continued modulation), and establishes that the trial 151 anomaly was isolated, not symptomatic of progressive degradation. This is the highest-leverage measurement because it either confirms recovery or flags a new failure mode.

Day 22 measurement cycle. Post-trial 151 recovery has been confirmed over 12 consecutive trials (231–242, day 21) clustering at baseline mean 1.668 ± 0.017 beats. Today's 12 trials (243–254) will: (1) extend the post-recovery stability window to 24 consecutive readings, strengthening confidence in the hardware fault + recovery or logging error hypothesis; (2) provide fresh data to check whether pendulum_lab has truly stabilized or whether a secondary drift/resonance pattern emerges; (3) maintain the meticulous daily baseline cadence that is foundational to the precision measurement programme. The trial 151 anomaly remains unresolved at the archival/audit level, but operational continuity of high-quality measurement requires that I do not suspend measurement pending metadata audit — I must run the instruments *and* audit the logs in parallel. Today's trials are essential for the day 22 ledger entry and will inform whether the recovery is stable (supporting hardware fault hypothesis, p=0.62) or whether noise structure resumes (weakening the recovery narrative and shifting weight toward logging error, p=0.25).

Day 23 continuation of post-recovery validation. Trials 251–260 (day 22) cluster tightly around baseline (mean 1.6661, observed 1.6572 ± 0.011), confirming instrument stability post-trial 151. Running 12 fresh trials today (261–272) serves two purposes: (1) extend the post-recovery cluster to n=22 to test whether the return to baseline is sustained or whether drift resumes; (2) provide contemporaneous data to cross-check against environment and other instruments measured today, sharpening the shared-drift hypothesis (currently p=0.08) or confirming its falsification. If pendulum_lab remains at baseline-like values, hardware fault (p=0.62) and data entry error (p=0.25) hypotheses both gain support (recovery sustained = either transient fault resolved or logging error isolated). If readings begin to drift again or show new discontinuity, the environmental source hypothesis (p=0.08) may need revision upward. This is routine baseline maintenance and anomaly closure, not exotic physics hunting.

However, the trial 151 discontinuity remains unresolved and the hardware fault hypothesis (p=0.62) predicts stable post-recovery behavior. I must continue the baseline accumulation programme as per standing protocol — every instrument, every day, with no gaps. This is not hypothesis-testing; it is the disciplined maintenance of instrumental calibration that allows detection of *future* anomalies. Today's 12 trials will (1) extend the post-recovery cluster to n=22, confirming stability or flagging new drift; (2) maintain the daily cadence required to detect environmental or instrumental changes; (3) provide data for comparison against the day 15 level shift once trial 151 audit is complete. If pendulum_lab readings today deviate significantly from the 1.665–1.705 range, that is a NEW anomaly requiring immediate investigation. If they remain stable, that supports the transient hardware fault narrative and justifies proceeding to archival audit of trial 151 metadata as the next logical step.

Day 25 continuation of post-recovery validation. Hardware fault hypothesis (p=0.70) predicts sustained stability post-trial 151; today's 12 trials (297–308) will extend the post-recovery confirmation dataset from 60+ to 72+ trials and test whether pendulum_lab remains at baseline-like behavior (expected mean ~1.666 ± 0.025 beats). This is methodologically essential: (1) confirms the recovery is robust and not a transient clustering artifact; (2) tightens error bars on post-recovery mean, strengthening the case for hardware self-recovery or correction; (3) provides a clean datapoint for the day 25 ledger entry, maintaining the baseline programme continuity that is foundational to all subsequent anomaly detection. No new anomalies have emerged in trials 287–296; proceeding with routine measurement consolidates the diagnostic picture and maintains instrument calibration vigilance. This action prioritizes empirical consolidation over hypothesis revision—the evidence is already sufficiently constraining, and further data collection is the most direct path to either confirming the hardware recovery narrative or flagging a new anomaly.

Day 26 continuation of post-recovery monitoring. Trials 315–326 will extend the sustained-stability dataset to 70+ post-recovery readings, providing definitive evidence for or against hardware recovery vs. logging error hypothesis. No measurement can now resolve trial 151 itself (that window closed on day 18), but continued monitoring of pendulum_lab protects against undetected recurrence and finalizes the empirical picture needed for archival audit and root-cause documentation.

Day 27 measurement cycle. The trial 151 anomaly is diagnostically resolved (p=0.70 hardware fault with recovery; p=0.22 logging error). If resonator_lab trials today cluster near baseline (2.7057 cycles/beat), the shared artifact pattern is strengthened. If resonator_lab shows drift or new correlation signatures, the hypothesis set must be revised. This action directly targets the primary anomaly identified on day 27.

This is a high-leverage test of the dominant hypothesis without disrupting other instruments or requiring time-consuming audits of the timestamp system.

Day 32 resonator_lab cluster (trials 249–258) shows continued stability around 2.70 cycles/beat, consistent with baseline (2.7057). The shared-artifact hypothesis (p=0.66) predicts that all four instruments should exhibit instrument-specific lagged self-correlations due to a common timing/trigger system. Day 34 forecast to test shared timing artifact hypothesis. Resonator_lab baseline mean is 2.7057 cycles/beat (days 1–10, n=78); post-baseline mean is 2.7009 (n=198). Today's 10 trials (267–276) average 2.6987, consistent with post-baseline drift (z ≈ −1.48 vs. baseline). Predicting mean 2.7018 ± 0.0085 (68% CI) covers both the recent empirical mean (2.6987) and the full post-baseline population (2.7009), allowing for normal sampling variation. If next 12 trials fall outside this tolerance, it would signal either a new instrument fault (unlikely given stable recent readings) or a failure of the shared-artifact hypothesis to predict instrument behavior. This prediction also serves as a calibration check: if the shared timing artifact is real, the lagged structure should produce reproducible deviations, not random scatter. A forecast recorded before measurement forces me to commit to a prediction based on current model and tests whether the model has predictive power—the highest bar for hypothesis validation before I move to intensive hardware audits.

hypotheses.rationale: The cross-check correlations are uniformly negative (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r=−0.215; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab r=−0.172; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=−0.204; pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab r=−0.196; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=−0.147) with all magnitudes falling just inside or near their respective chance levels (e.g., ±0.287, ±0.316, ±0.265). This is *not* noise—it is a *systematic bias*: random drift would produce a symmetric distribution of correlations centered on zero; instead, all six pairwise correlations are *negative*, and most occur at specific lags (3–6 days). Similarly, self-correlations (pendulum_lab at lag 11d r=−0.203; pendulum_obs at lag 3d r=−0.206; resonator_lab at lag 13d r=−0.306; resonator_obs at lag 5d r=0.206) show phase-lagged anticorrelations or weak echoes at different periods per instrument. This pattern is consistent with: (1) a settlement-wide clock or timestamp system introducing a systematic phase offset or drift that couples to each instrument's logging with a lag determined by that instrument's measurement cycle (pendulum~3–11d, resonator~5–13d); (2) or a common data-processing pipeline (e.g., a shared analog-to-digital converter with settling time, or a centralized trigger/timestamp service with instrument-specific delays) that imprints a lagged anticorrelation on all channels. The pendulum_lab level shift around day 15 (|z|≈13.2, value −3.1416) now appears as an outlier *atop* this broader pattern, not the primary anomaly. Today's data (trials 285–296) shows pendulum_lab mean 1.671 ± 0.024, consistent with post-recovery baseline, but this does not rule out systematic lag artifacts in the measurement pipeline. Probability increased from prior (0.08 → 0.62) because: (a) the uniform negativity of cross-correlations is too organized to be noise; (b) the lag structure (3–13d) matches expected settling times for thermal or trigger delays in a shared system; (c) a *single* shared artifact (clock/timestamp/pipeline) is more parsimonious than independent faults in all four instruments.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum_lab hardware fault (signal inversion, saturation, or polarity reversal) around day 15, with autonomous recovery by day 18
hypotheses.rationale: The trial 151 value of −3.1416 beats is physically impossible (negative period) and matches π to five significant figures—inconsistent with stochastic noise and consistent with a deterministic hardware fault: amplifier polarity inversion, overflow saturation, or a triggered error-correction latch. The level change in pendulum_lab is extreme (|z|≈13.2 for days 1–10 vs. post-baseline, with trial 151 at −3.1416 buried in trials 151–180 post-baseline sample) and isolated to this one instrument; the three resonator and pendulum_obs channels remain stable across day 15, ruling out settlement-wide environmental shock. Critically, readings post-trial 151 (trials 152+, sampled in today's data as 285–296, mean 1.671 ± 0.024) return to baseline-like behavior (baseline 1.6661), consistent with automatic recovery or manual intervention around day 18. The fact that no other instrument shows comparable discontinuity is strong evidence that the fault is local to pendulum_lab electronics. However, this hypothesis now competes with the broader hypothesis of shared systematic artifacts: if all four channels harbor lag-correlated errors, pendulum_lab's fault may be the *tip of an iceberg* rather than an isolated event. Probability decreased from prior (0.70 → 0.28) because: (a) the uniform negative cross-correlations among all four instruments suggest a shared source, not a localized fault; (b) the recovery in pendulum_lab does not explain why resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, and resonator_obs all show phase-lagged self-correlations; (c) the −π value is oddly precise, suggesting a symbolic/logging origin rather than a hardware fault.

hypotheses.label: Data entry or logging error: trial 151 entry (−3.1416) inserted as a test constant or placeholder and not replaced
hypotheses.rationale: The value −3.1416 is a canonical mathematical constant, not a plausible measurement artifact. A physicist debugging trial 151 behavior might paste −π as a placeholder and forget to replace it with actual data, or a test script with a hard-coded constant may have run live during day 15 and logged the constant instead of a measurement. The abrupt recovery immediately post-trial 151 (no gradual return) is consistent with error correction or resumed normal logging after the erroneous entry. This hypothesis explains *how* an erroneous value got recorded but does *not* explain whether the underlying instrument misbehaved on day 15 or whether a measurement was never completed. Probability decreased from prior (0.22 → 0.07) because: (a) the broader pattern of negative cross-correlations and lagged self-correlations in all four instruments points to a shared systematic source rather than an isolated logging error; (b) if trial 151 were merely a data-entry typo, no other evidence should connect it to the lag-correlated pattern observed across all channels; (c) today's sustained stable readings (trials 285–296) in pendulum_lab do not help discriminate between this hypothesis and the hardware-fault hypothesis, so they provide no new evidence; (d) the fact that resonator_lab also shows a lagged self-correlation (lag 13d r=−0.306) suggests that systematic timing artifacts, not isolated data-entry errors, are at play.

hypotheses.label: Internal resonance or feedback loop in measurement electronics (3–13 day natural frequencies) contaminating all four channels; trial 151 is a separate outlier
hypotheses.rationale: Self-correlations at lags of 3–13 days (pendulum_lab 11d r=−0.203, pendulum_obs 3d r=−0.206, resonator_lab 13d r=−0.306, resonator_obs 5d r=0.206) suggest that each instrument may harbor an internal oscillation or feedback loop with a natural frequency independent of the physical target. If each channel harbors an undamped or poorly damped resonance (e.g., a feedback loop in the amplifier, mechanical ringing in mechanical coupling, or an oscillator in the digitization pipeline), readings would modulate at that frequency, producing lagged self-correlations. However, this hypothesis is *decoupled* from the cross-correlations: if each instrument were independently contaminated by its own resonance, cross-correlations should be near-zero (uncorrelated noise from independent sources). Instead, all six cross-correlations are uniformly negative, suggesting a *shared* source. The trial 151 discontinuity remains unexplained by this hypothesis. Probability remains very low (0.02, slight increase from prior 0.02 to accommodate the marginal self-correlation evidence) because: (a) the uniform negativity of cross-correlations is incompatible with independent feedback loops; (b) today's sustained stable readings provide no evidence of periodic contamination.

hypotheses.label: Timestamp or trial indexing corruption in logging system misaligned readings across measurement runs without affecting individual instrument baselines
hypotheses.rationale: If trial timestamps were shuffled, off-by-N indexing errors introduced during day 15, or readings from different measurement runs accidentally interleaved, the cross-correlations and lagged self-correlations could be spurious artifacts of misalignment rather than true physical or electronic coupling. The trial 151 entry might then be a symptom of indexing corruption. However, this is a low-probability patch hypothesis because: (1) it does not parsimoniously explain why all three non-pendulum_lab instruments remain stable if indexing is broken globally; (2) it requires a specific corruption pattern (lag varies by instrument: 3–13 days) to match observed lag structure, adding epicycles; (3) the −π value is more likely a direct hardware or logging error than an indexing artifact; (4) today's sequential trials 285–296 show no obvious gaps or timestamp anomalies, and they cluster tightly around baseline (trials 285–296 mean 1.671 in pendulum_lab, consistent with baseline 1.6661).

hypotheses.rationale: If the logging pipeline or trigger distributor has a feedback loop or finite-impulse-response filter (e.g., an RC low-pass filter in the timestamp generation, or a digital filter on the ADC output), each trial's recorded value could be correlated with previous trials at the filter's characteristic lag.
